sentences.text: This dinosaur is named Lirainosaurus, which translates to slender lizard in Basque and Greek, reflecting its thin build.
It was a relatively small sauropod, with a length ranging from 4 to 6 meters and a mass between 2 to 4 metric tons.
Only two fragmentary osteoderms have been discovered, indicating it had less extensive armor than titanosaurians like Ampelosaurus.
The animal possessed teeth shaped like pins, a feature distinct from many other large herbivores.
Due to extensive descriptions of its fossils, Lirainosaurus was the most studied titanosaur in Europe in 2015.
The type species Lirainosaurus astibiae was described by Sanz and colleagues in 1999.
The genus was originally defined based on a skull fragment, teeth, vertebrae, and limb bones found in Laño, northern Spain.
By 2015, researchers reported that 150 bones had been recovered from Lirainosaurus sites.
There are 10 recorded fossil occurrences of Lirainosaurus in the Paleobiology Database.
Fossils of Lirainosaurus have been found at the Bellevue site in the northern Pyrenees.
Contemporaneous dinosaurs at the Bellevue site included the titanosaur Ampelosaurus, the hadrosaur Rhabdodon, and indeterminate ankylosaurian and dromaeosaurid elements.
A 2016 study suggested Lirainosaurus was phylogenetically closer to Alamosaurus and Opisthocoelicaudia than to Saltasaurus.
In 2018, Diez Diaz and colleagues created the subfamily Lirainosaurinae to include Lirainosaurus, Ampelosaurus, and Atsinganosaurus.
Lirainosaurus belongs to the parent group Lirainosaurinae.
Lirainosaurus is classified in the class Saurischia.
Lirainosaurus lived between the Late Campanian and Early Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
Lirainosaurus shared its environment with Ampelosaurus, Rhabdodon, ankylosaurs, and dromaeosaurids.
Marine biostratigraphic tests place the age of the formation containing Lirainosaurus fossils between the late Campanian and early Maastrichtian.
Local stratigraphy at the Fox-Amphoux-Métisson site shows the same facies succession as the Aix-en-Provence basin, dating to the late Campanian to early Maastrichtian.
Lirainosaurus lived from 83.6 to 66 million years ago during the Campanian to Maastrichtian.
